planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; mangkokan is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; mangkokan is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Round, cupped, saucer-shaped leaves with scalloped edges give this Southeast Asian shrub its common name, and the young, tender leaves are eaten raw as a salad green or wrapped around other foods in Indonesian and Malaysian cooking, traditionally valued for supporting milk production in nursing mothers. Easy to grow and propagate from stem cuttings, it tolerates the light shade beneath larger trees or shrubs and produces usable leaves within a few months of rooting, making it a practical addition to a warm-climate edible landscape. Harvest young leaves continuously as needed, and protect from any frost, since cold quickly damages or kills the plant.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pak Wan is frost-tender and slow-growing, realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a container plant brought indoors for winter.

directions: Plant seedlings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pak Wan is frost-tender and slow-growing, realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a container plant brought indoors for winter. Native to Thailand and mainland Southeast Asia, this small tree produces tender young shoots and leaves prized as one of the most highly regarded wild vegetables in Thai cuisine, with a naturally sweet flavor (giving the plant its Thai name, which translates as 'sweet vegetable') typically stir-fried or added to soups and omelets. It grows slowly and can take several years to reach a size worth regular harvesting, and it has historically been difficult to propagate and cultivate outside its native range, so wild-collected shoots remain more common than cultivated ones even within Thailand. Harvest young, tender shoot tips regularly once the plant is established, and provide the warm, humid, partly shaded forest-edge conditions of its native habitat for the best growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant divisions after last frost in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade near a support to climb; Paku Miding is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant divisions after last frost in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade near a support to climb; Paku Miding is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Unlike most edible ferns, this Southeast Asian species climbs by scrambling over shrubs and trees in swampy forest, and its young, tender, reddish fiddleheads and shoot tips are harvested as a popular vegetable across Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, typically stir-fried with garlic and chili or added to soups. It thrives in the same wet, swampy, semi-shaded conditions favored by many tropical wetland edibles, spreading by rhizome in consistently moist to wet soil at a pond margin or bog garden. Harvest young shoot tips regularly to encourage continued production, and provide a trellis or nearby shrub for the scrambling fronds to climb.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating. This large Southeast Asian rainforest tree produces football-sized fruit containing large seeds that, after a traditional fermentation and boiling process to remove naturally occurring toxic compounds, become the famous kluwak or keluak used to flavor the dark, earthy Indonesian dish rawon and Peranakan ayam buah keluak. The raw seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic and must never be eaten without proper traditional processing, which involves burying, boiling, and fermenting the seeds over an extended period to render them safe. Grow only as a specialty tree for a large tropical property or botanical collection, and never attempt to process or consume the fruit without expert traditional knowledge of the detoxification method.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant divisions after last frost into rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water in full sun; yellow velvetleaf spreads readily by seed and runners in warm, wet conditions and is best grown in a contained bog bed or submerged container.

directions: Plant divisions after last frost into rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water in full sun; yellow velvetleaf spreads readily by seed and runners in warm, wet conditions and is best grown in a contained bog bed or submerged container. Broad, glossy, velvety-textured leaves rise on long stalks from the shallow water of rice paddies and wetlands across Southeast Asia, where the young leaves and flower stalks are harvested as a popular cooked vegetable, and cheerful three-petaled yellow flowers add ornamental value above the foliage. It grows and spreads quickly in warm, wet, nutrient-rich conditions, making it a fast-establishing addition to a pond margin or paddy-style bed, but its vigorous self-seeding habit means it can become weedy in the very rice paddies it is sometimes intentionally grown alongside. Harvest young leaves and flower stalks regularly for the best eating quality, and confine plantings to a contained wet bed to prevent unwanted spread.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant divisions after last frost into wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; Semanggi spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container or contained bog bed.

directions: Plant divisions after last frost into wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; Semanggi spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container or contained bog bed. Small, four-lobed leaves resembling a four-leaf clover float or stand just above the mud of rice paddies and shallow wetlands across Indonesia, where the tender young leaves and stems are harvested and traditionally steamed as the key ingredient in the East Javanese dish pecel semanggi, tossed with a spicy peanut sauce. This true fern (not a clover, despite the resemblance) spreads readily by creeping rhizomes across wet mud, forming a low, dense mat useful for the shallow-water margin of a bog garden or paddy-style planting. Harvest young leaves and stems regularly for the best eating quality, and keep the planting confined to prevent it from spreading beyond the intended wet area.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
